Matrix preconditioning (M−1/2AM−1/2)

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Numerical linear algebra OurBigBook.com
Matrix preconditioning transforms a linear system using an inexpensive auxiliary solve to improve its eigenvalues. For symmetric positive-definite matrices, a symmetric positive-definite matrix M produces M−1/2AM−1/2, preserving the symmetric structure needed by the Conjugate gradient method.
A useful matrix preconditioner combines a cheap solve with favorable transformed eigenvalues; neither property alone is enough.[ref]
The aim is to make each correction more effective without making it expensive. The example under diagonal scaling for a two-dimensional linear system turns thin ellipses into nearly circular ones and makes preconditioned steepest descent effective.

Matrix preconditioner (M)

Words: 222 Articles: 1
Matrix preconditioning OurBigBook.com
A matrix preconditioner is an auxiliary invertible matrix whose matrix inverse is cheap to apply and whose use improves the eigenvalues of a linear system. In symmetric positive-definite matrix problems, a symmetric positive-definite matrix M preserves that structure under the symmetric transformation M−1/2AM−1/2.
Applying M−1 means solving Mz=r for a supplied vector r. This notation does not require forming a general matrix inverse. A diagonal matrix gives componentwise divisions; a factored matrix gives auxiliary solves such as forward substitution and back substitution.[ref]
Choosing M=I makes the solve trivial but changes nothing; choosing M=A gives the exact correction but asks us to solve the original linear system.[ref]

Jacobi preconditioner (M=diag(a11​,…,ann​))

Words: 87
Matrix preconditioner OurBigBook.com
The Jacobi preconditioner keeps only the diagonal entries of the matrix A. For a symmetric positive-definite matrix, these entries are positive, so its auxiliary solve is zi​=ri​/aii​. It rescales coordinates with very different diagonal sizes, but cannot remove arbitrary off-diagonal coupling.[ref]
This shares a diagonal matrix with the Jacobi method, but the roles differ. The Jacobi method specifies a whole stationary iterative method for a linear system; a Jacobi preconditioner supplies an auxiliary solve to another iterative method, including the Preconditioned conjugate gradient method.

Left preconditioning (M−1Ax=M−1b)

Words: 70
Matrix preconditioning OurBigBook.com
Left preconditioning multiplies both sides of the linear system Ax=b by the same invertible matrix M−1. It leaves the unknown vector x unchanged. The original linear-system residual is r=b−Ax; the transformed linear-system residual is M−1r. Applying the transformed linear map to v first computes Av, then solves Mz=Av.
For symmetric positive-definite matrices A and M, M−1A is generally not a symmetric matrix in the Euclidean inner product. Its positive eigenvalues alone do not justify ordinary Euclidean Conjugate gradient method recurrences. The remedy is symmetric positive-definite preconditioning, implemented through the Preconditioned conjugate gradient method.

Right preconditioning (AM−1u=b,x=M−1u)

Words: 75
Matrix preconditioning OurBigBook.com
Right preconditioning substitutes x=M−1u into the linear system Ax=b. Applying its transformed linear map first solves Mz=v, then computes Az. Recover the solution by solving Mx=u. Its linear-system residual b−AM−1u is exactly the original linear-system residual b−Ax, which is useful when monitoring the imbalance in the original equations.
The left preconditioning and right preconditioning transformed matrices are similar matrices:
AM−1=M(M−1A)M−1.
(1)
They therefore have the same eigenvalues, although their Euclidean norm condition numbers and residual histories need not agree. A similarity transformation preserves eigenvalues; a nonorthogonal change of coordinates need not preserve lengths.

Symmetric positive-definite preconditioning (B=M−1/2AM−1/2,y=M1/2x)

Words: 383 Articles: 1
Matrix preconditioning OurBigBook.com
Let A and M be real symmetric positive-definite matrices. The principal square root of a positive semidefinite matrix construction gives an invertible matrix for each. Set
S=M1/2,B=S−1AS−1,y=Sx,c=S−1b.
(2)
Then Ax=b is equivalent to By=c. This is a matrix congruence, and B is a symmetric positive-definite matrix: BT=B, and for every nonzero vector v,
vTBv=(S−1v)TA(S−1v)>0,
(3)
since S−1v=0. This short proof establishes both requirements for applying the Conjugate gradient method to the transformed linear system.
The left transformed matrix has the same eigenvalues because
M−1A=S−1BS.
(4)
Its correct geometry uses the weighted inner product ⟨u,v⟩M​=uTMv: ⟨u,M−1Av⟩M​=uTAv=⟨M−1Au,v⟩M​. Thus it is symmetric in this inner product, even when it is not a symmetric matrix in ordinary coordinates. The spectral condition number governing the transformed symmetric problem is κ2​(B), not generally κ2​(M−1A).
The Preconditioned conjugate gradient method realizes this transformation using auxiliary solves Mzk​=rk​, without constructing S or its matrix inverse. With fixed M, initialize r0​=b−Ax0​ and p0​=z0​; while rk​=0, use
αk​=pkT​Apk​rkT​zk​​,xk+1​=xk​+αk​pk​,rk+1​=rk​−αk​Apk​,
(5)
then solve Mzk+1​=rk+1​ and set
βk​=rkT​zk​rk+1T​zk+1​​,pk+1​=zk+1​+βk​pk​.
(6)
Stop at a zero linear-system residual before forming another ratio. Positive definiteness makes the denominators positive before termination.[ref]
An invertible matrix alone is insufficient: with A=I and M=diag(−1,1), the left transformed matrix has eigenvalues −1,1, and M has no real symmetric positive-definite matrix square root. Even a valid symmetric positive-definite matrix can worsen conditioning if its scaling is unsuitable, as the next worked example shows.

Symmetric preconditioning as energy geometry (∥x−x∗​∥A​=∥M1/2(x−x∗​)∥B​)

Words: 157
Symmetric positive-definite preconditioning OurBigBook.com
For a symmetric positive-definite matrix A, solving Ax∗​=b is equivalent to minimizing the quadratic form with linear term
F(x)=21​xTAx−bTx.
(7)
Writing the error vector e=x−x∗​ and expanding gives the exact energy norm identity
F(x)−F(x∗​)=21​eTAe=21​∥e∥A2​.
(8)
The cross term vanishes because Ax∗​=b. With η=Se and B=S−1AS−1, the same quantity is ηTBη/2. Symmetric positive-definite preconditioning changes coordinates without changing the energy assigned to a corresponding error vector.
In an orthonormal eigenbasis of A, the level set eTAe=t>0 has semiaxis lengths t/λi​​. Its longest-to-shortest axis ratio is κ2​(A)​. A large spectral condition number of a positive-definite matrix therefore appears geometrically as a thin ellipsoid. Good scaling makes the transformed ellipsoid rounder, allowing a simple search direction to improve all coordinates together.
The negative gradient of F is the linear-system residual r. Relative to the norm ∥v∥M​=vTMv​, a steepest direction is z=M−1r: the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to rTv=(S−1r)T(Sv) shows that the greatest decrease per unit M-length occurs along this direction. Equivalently, ordinary gradient descent in y=Sx becomes preconditioned steepest descent in x.[ref]

Diagonal scaling for a two-dimensional linear system (κ2​(B)=51/49)

Words: 194
Matrix preconditioning OurBigBook.com
Consider the original linear system
A=(11/5​1/5100​),b=(11​),M=(10​0100​).
(9)
Completing the square proves that A is a symmetric positive-definite matrix:
eTAe=(e1​+e2​/5)2+252499​e22​>0(e=0).
(10)
The Jacobi preconditioner M has S=diag(1,10). Symmetric positive-definite preconditioning gives
B=(11/50​1/501​),c=(11/10​).
(11)
Its eigenvectors (1,1)T and (1,−1)T have eigenvalues 51/50 and 49/50. Hence
κ2​(B)=4951​≈1.040816.
(12)
The characteristic polynomial of A is λ2−101λ+2499/25. Its eigenvalues and spectral condition number of a positive-definite matrix are
λ±​=10505±245029​​,κ2​(A)=λ−​λ+​​≈100.040824.
(13)
The ellipse axis ratio drops from about 10.0020 to 1.0202. The transformation multiplies the second coordinate by ten, bringing the two energy scales together.
Both panels show the same energy level sets, expressed in error coordinates e=x−x∗​ and η=M1/2e. Their coordinate axes have equal scales. The marked displacement (1,0.1)T becomes (1,1)T; its energy remains eTAe/2=1.02. These are exact contours of the specified quadratic form.
Solving the original equations gives
x∗​=24991​(249520​),y∗​=24991​(2495200​).
(14)
Direct matrix multiplication checks both linear-system residuals:
Ax∗​=24991​(2495+4499+2000​)=b,By∗​=24991​(2495+4499/10+200​)=c.
(15)
By contrast, left preconditioning gives M−1A=(11/500​1/51​), which is visibly not a symmetric matrix, despite having the same positive eigenvalues as B.
A bad scaling can reverse the benefit: the still valid symmetric positive-definite matrix Mbad​=diag(100,1) gives Bbad​=(1/1001/50​1/50100​). Its Rayleigh quotients on the coordinate unit vectors are 0.01 and 100, so κ2​(Bbad​)≥10000. Cheapness and positive definiteness do not guarantee improved conditioning.

Preconditioned steepest descent (Mzk​=rk​,αk​=rkT​zk​/(zkT​Azk​))

Words: 447 Articles: 1
Matrix preconditioning OurBigBook.com
For fixed symmetric positive-definite matrices A and M, preconditioned steepest descent minimizes F(x)=xTAx/2−bTx along the direction supplied by the auxiliary solve. Given xk​, form the linear-system residual rk​=b−Axk​. If rk​=0, stop: xk​=x∗​. Otherwise solve Mzk​=rk​ and use
αk​=zkT​Azk​rkT​zk​​,xk+1​=xk​+αk​zk​,rk+1​=rk​−αk​Azk​.
(16)
This is exact line search for a positive-definite quadratic along zk​. Indeed,
F(xk​+αzk​)=F(xk​)−αrkT​zk​+21​α2zkT​Azk​,
(17)
whose derivative vanishes at the displayed positive step size. Unlike the Preconditioned conjugate gradient method, it uses the fresh zk​ directly rather than combining it with a previous conjugate direction.
For diagonal scaling for a two-dimensional linear system, start at x0​=0. Without matrix preconditioning, take M=I: z0​=(1,1)T, α0​=10/507, and
x1​=5071​(1010​),r1​=169165​(1−1​).
(18)
With the Jacobi preconditioner M=diag(1,100), z0​=(1,1/100)T, α0​=505/507, and
x1​=(505/507101/10140​),r1​=(33/16900−33/169​).
(19)
The original linear-system residual becomes much smaller after this correction. Quantify progress in the same energy norm in both cases: Ek​=F(xk​)−F(x∗​) and E0​=2515/4998. Exact substitution gives
E0​E1​​=qI​=8500781675​≈0.960803228,E0​E1(M)​​=qM​=85007003267​≈0.000384321291.
(20)
In this particular example the entire histories are Ek​/E0​=qIk​ and Ek(M)​/E0​=qMk​. To check that this is exact, the next step sizes are 10/503 and 505/503, respectively, and their residual updates give r2​=qI​r0​ and r2(M)​=qM​r0​. Multiplying a linear-system residual by a nonzero scalar leaves the next step size unchanged; every pair of steps repeats the same directions at a smaller scale. The two first-step energy ratios then establish these formulas for all k.
The curves come from exact rational updates of the specified linear system, converted to decimal values for plotting. The left panel counts iterations. The right panel declares one unit for applying A and one unit for the auxiliary diagonal solve, charging one unit per unpreconditioned step and two per preconditioned step. It excludes setup and vector operations, so it compares a declared cost model rather than measured runtime. Scaling is advantageous even with that extra charge.
These curves compare steepest descent method iterations. On this two-dimensional linear system, both the Conjugate gradient method and the Preconditioned conjugate gradient method terminate within two steps in exact arithmetic. The plot therefore establishes no CG iteration-count advantage for this example; the benefit of scaling for larger problems depends on their eigenvalues and auxiliary-solve costs.

Condition-number bound for preconditioned steepest descent (Ek+1​≤((κ−1)/(κ+1))2Ek​)

Words: 130
Preconditioned steepest descent OurBigBook.com
Let m=λmin​(B)>0, L=λmax​(B) and κ=L/m=κ2​(B) for the transformed symmetric positive-definite matrix. Then preconditioned steepest descent satisfies
Ek+1​≤(κ+1κ−1​)2Ek​.
(21)
This is a worst-case bound, not necessarily the actual rate. For our scaled example the bound is (1/50)2=0.0004, slightly above its computed factor qM​≈0.000384321291. If the initial transformed error is an eigenvector, exact line search for a positive-definite quadratic removes it in one step, regardless of the full condition number.
A short proof compares exact line search for a positive-definite quadratic with the trial step size α=2/(m+L) in the transformed coordinates. In an orthonormal eigenbasis of B, each error coefficient is multiplied by 1−αλi​, whose absolute value is at most (L−m)/(L+m). Summing λi​ times the squared coefficients bounds the trial energy by the square of this factor. The exact minimizing step size does at least as well. This also explains the terminating case m=L: the trial step removes the entire error in one iteration.

Power iteration (xk+1​=Axk​/∥Axk​∥2​)

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Numerical linear algebra OurBigBook.com
Power iteration finds a dominant eigenvalue and its eigenvector by repeatedly applying a matrix and rescaling the resulting vector. The essential idea is selective amplification: components along different eigenvectors grow at different rates, so one direction can eventually dominate. It is the computational form of the power method and is useful when applying a large sparse matrix to a vector is cheap but computing its whole spectral decomposition is expensive.
For a square matrix over the real numbers or complex numbers A, choose a unit vector x0​ and repeat
yk+1​=Axk​,xk+1​=∥yk+1​∥2​yk+1​​.
(22)
Here ∥⋅∥2​ is the Euclidean norm. If yk+1​=0, stop before division: the current vector is an eigenvector for the zero eigenvalue, and this iteration cannot continue. Otherwise, in exact arithmetic,
xk​=∥Akx0​∥2​Akx0​​.
(23)
Repeated normalization keeps the stored vectors at manageable size without changing their directions; it does not guarantee that an individual multiplication cannot exceed the range of floating-point arithmetic. The dominant eigenvalue means largest modulus, which need not mean largest signed real value.[ref]

Exact two-dimensional power iteration (tanθk​=3−k)

Words: 119
Power iteration OurBigBook.com
Consider the symmetric matrix and initial unit vector
A=(21​12​),x0​=(10​).
(24)
Its orthonormal eigenbasis consists of u1​=(1,1)T/2​ and u2​=(1,−1)T/2​, with eigenvalues 3 and 1. Since x0​=(u1​+u2​)/2​, direct multiplication gives
Akx0​=21​(3k+13k−1​),xk​=1+3−2k​u1​+3−ku2​​.
(25)
The first unnormalized vectors are (1,0)T, (2,1)T, (5,4)T, and (14,13)T. If θk​ is the acute angle from the line spanned by the dominant eigenvector, then tanθk​=3−k. Every application divides the unwanted-to-wanted component ratio by three: normalization changes lengths, while the spectral gap selects the direction.
The right panel compares the power iteration direction error, Rayleigh quotient error, and eigenpair residual. With tk​=3−k, their exact values are
εk​=1+tk2​​tk​​,3−ρk​=1+tk2​2tk2​​,∥rk​∥2​=1+tk2​2tk​​.
(26)
Thus a very accurate Rayleigh quotient can appear well before the eigenvector is comparably accurate. This is an example of quadratic Rayleigh-quotient improvement for the power method.

Power iteration convergence for a diagonalizable matrix (∣λ1​∣>∣λ2​∣,(V−1x0​)1​=0)

Words: 315 Articles: 1
Power iteration OurBigBook.com
Suppose A∈Cn×n is a diagonalizable matrix, n≥2, with an eigenbasis v1​,…,vn​ and spectral decomposition
A=VΛV−1,V=(v1​ ⋯ vn​),Λ=diag(λ1​,…,λn​).
(27)
Assume the dominant eigenvalue λ1​ is a simple eigenvalue and
∣λ1​∣>∣λ2​∣≥⋯≥∣λn​∣,x0​=∑j=1n​cj​vj​,c1​=0.
(28)
Then the normalized power iteration approaches the one-dimensional eigenspace of λ1​. Its asymptotic direction-error bound has factor γ=∣λ2​/λ1​∣<1. This spectral gap is a gap in modulus: if g=∣λ1​∣−∣λ2​∣, then γ=1−g/∣λ1​∣. A small relative gap gives slow convergence.[ref]
The short proof is the exact eigenbasis identity
c1​λ1k​Akx0​​=v1​+∑j=2n​c1​cj​​(λ1​λj​​)kvj​.
(29)
The remaining sum has norm bounded by a constant times γk. This proves convergence of direction, allowing a changing sign or complex factor. A tiny c1​ or a poorly conditioned, nonorthogonal eigenbasis can delay visible convergence: the condition number of V affects constants, while γ controls the eventual rate. The bound need not be an equality; if the initial coefficient of the second-largest eigenvalue vanishes, the active spectrum of the power method gives a faster rate. When γ=0, all unwanted components disappear after one multiplication.[ref]
The hypothesis is c1​=(V−1x0​)1​=0, not an ordinary nonzero inner product with the right eigenvector. Let w1∗​ be the first row of V−1, a left eigenvector normalized so w1∗​vj​ is 1 for j=1 and 0 otherwise; ∗ denotes conjugate transpose. Then c1​=w1∗​x0​. For a Hermitian matrix, choose an orthonormal eigenbasis and the criterion becomes v1∗​x0​=0: the starting vector must be nonorthogonal to the dominant eigenvector. For a general diagonalizable matrix, the nonorthogonal eigenbasis makes these two tests different, as illustrated under power iteration failure cases.

Power iteration direction error (εk​=∥(I−uu∗)xk​∥2​)

Words: 81
Power iteration convergence for a diagonalizable matrix OurBigBook.com
For a unit vector u spanning the target eigenspace and a normalized iterate xk​, define
εk​=∥(I−uu∗)xk​∥2​=1−∣u∗xk​∣2​.
(30)
This is the norm of the component in the orthogonal complement of u, equivalently the sine of the acute angle to its line. It ignores the arbitrary sign or complex unit factor of an eigenvector. Under power iteration convergence for a diagonalizable matrix, εk​=O(γk) in Big O notation. The orthogonal projection defines how we measure direction; it does not assume that the eigenbasis of A is orthogonal. In computation, the projection form avoids subtracting nearly equal numbers inside the square root.

Sign and phase in power iteration (xk​=∣c1​λ1k​∣c1​λ1k​​u1​+O(γk))

Words: 159
Power iteration OurBigBook.com
Under power iteration convergence for a diagonalizable matrix, take v1​=u1​ to be a unit vector. The displayed formula describes both the dominant eigenvector direction and its rotating complex unit factor. With real data and a positive dominant eigenvalue, xk​ converges to u1​ or −u1​ according to the sign of c1​. With a negative dominant eigenvalue, consecutive vectors approach opposite signs even though their power iteration direction error tends to zero.
For complex data write λ1​=∣λ1​∣eiϕ, where ϕ is its complex argument. The leading factor turns by eiϕ per step, so the vectors generally do not converge. For example, A=diag(2i,1) and x0​=(1,1)T/2​ give Akx0​=((2i)k,1)T/2​: the first component cycles through four phases while the ratio of component moduli tends to zero. Its power iteration direction error is 2−k/1+2−2k​. Multiplying xk​ by e−i(argc1​+kϕ) gives a sequence converging to u1​.
A stopping rule based only on ∥xk+1​−xk​∥2​ therefore rejects successful sign-alternating iterations. A comparison invariant under complex unit factors is
min∣ω∣=1​∥xk+1​−ωxk​∥2​=2−2∣xk∗​xk+1​∣​.
(31)
Even this comparison can be small for a slowly changing wrong mixture; the eigenpair residual supplies a separate diagnostic.

Power iteration eigenpair diagnostics (ρk​=xk∗​Axk​,rk​=Axk​−ρk​xk​)

Words: 183
Power iteration OurBigBook.com
For each unit vector iterate compute the Rayleigh quotient ρk​=xk∗​Axk​ and the eigenpair residual rk​=Axk​−ρk​xk​. Use the same multiplication Axk​ for both diagnostics and the next normalized iterate. For any complex matrix, this Rayleigh quotient minimizes ∥Axk​−μxk​∥2​ over complex scalars μ, because xk∗​rk​=0. Under power iteration convergence for a diagonalizable matrix, ρk​→λ1​ and ∥rk​∥2​→0, even when the vectors alternate signs or phases.[ref]
A dimensionless stopping quantity is
ηk​=∥A∥2​+∣ρk​∣∥rk​∥2​​,
(32)
when the denominator is positive; ∥A∥2​ is the operator norm, and a known upper bound may replace it if computing it is costly. A small eigenpair residual certifies a small backward error of an approximate eigenpair, but does not establish that the eigenvalue found is dominant.
For a Hermitian matrix with orthonormal eigenbasis uj​, write xk​=∑j​aj​uj​. Then the independently useful identity
∥rk​∥22​=∑j​∣aj​∣2∣λj​−ρk​∣2
(33)
shows that some eigenvalue lies within ∥rk​∥2​ of ρk​. If a specific target eigenvalue λ1​ is separated from all the others by δk​=minj>1​∣λj​−ρk​∣>0, it also gives εk​≤∥rk​∥2​/δk​. This separation is measured from the computed Rayleigh quotient; it differs from the dominant-modulus spectral gap. For a nonnormal matrix, the same orthogonal expansion is unavailable and a small eigenpair residual alone need not imply a comparably small distance to the spectrum.

Power iteration failure cases

Words: 272
Power iteration OurBigBook.com
A tied largest modulus can prevent even direction convergence. With D=diag(2,−2) and x0​=(1,1)T/2​,
xk​=2​1​(1(−1)k​),ρk​=0,∥rk​∥2​=2.
(34)
The two directions form a cycle; neither is an eigenvector. There is no dominant-modulus spectral gap. A tied modulus is not a universal failure: an initial eigenvector remains on its line, and A=2I preserves every direction. Subspace iteration addresses a separated cluster by targeting a dominant invariant subspace instead of one eigenvector.
An orthogonal start can fail despite a strict spectral gap. For A=(21​12​) and x0​=(1,−1)T/2​, the dominant component is zero, so Ax0​=x0​ and every iterate equals x0​. The Rayleigh quotient is exactly 1 and the eigenpair residual is zero, although the dominant eigenvalue is 3. Exact arithmetic never creates a missing component.[ref]

For a nonorthogonal eigenbasis, even the word “orthogonal” must be used carefully. The diagonalizable matrix C=(30​21​) has right eigenvectors v1​=(1,0)T, v2​=(−1,1)T, and dominant left eigenvector w1​=(1,1)T. For x0​=(a,b)T, the dominant coefficient is c1​=w1T​x0​=a+b. The starting vector v2​ is nonorthogonal to v1​ but stays at the smaller eigenvalue 1; (0,1)T is orthogonal to v1​ but has c1​=1 and converges to the dominant direction. The left eigenvector test, not the right-eigenvector inner product, controls the outcome.
A random vector drawn from a continuous probability distribution with a probability density function on the full real or complex vector space has c1​=0 with probability one. This avoids the exact missing-component hyperplane, but does not guarantee a large component or fast convergence. Floating-point arithmetic may seed a missing component, yet a structurally preserved zero can remain zero, so accidental perturbations are not a convergence guarantee.

Gaussian elimination

Words: 4k Articles: 25
Numerical linear algebra OurBigBook.com
Gaussian elimination applies elementary row operations to reduce a linear system to triangular form. Dense elimination uses O(n3) arithmetic operations.
Gaussian elimination solves a linear system by removing one unknown from later equations at each step. Write the coefficients and right-hand side together as an augmented matrix [A∣b]. Apply the same elementary row operations to both parts until the coefficients form a row echelon form; for a square invertible matrix, this gives an upper triangular matrix system. Then back substitution recovers the unknowns from the last equation upward. The useful simplification is that each successive equation involves fewer unknowns, while the set of solutions stays the same.
Why do elementary row operations preserve solutions? Interchanging equations changes only their order. Multiplying an equation by a nonzero scalar can be undone by division. Replacing equation i by itself plus c times equation j, with i=j, can be undone by adding −c times the unchanged equation j. Equivalently, an elementary matrix E is an invertible matrix, so Ax=b if and only if EAx=Eb. Applying an operation to A without also applying it to b loses this equivalence.
At step k, choose a nonzero pivot element akk​ after any row interchange. For every i>k, form the elimination multiplier mi​=aik​/akk​ and perform the elementary row operation Ri​←Ri​−mi​Rk​. Its coefficient in column k becomes aik​−(aik​/akk​)akk​=0 in exact arithmetic. Later operations combine rows that already have zeros in earlier columns, so those zeros survive. If an active column has no nonzero candidate, general row echelon form reduction skips it; a square invertible matrix always has a candidate at each step with suitable row interchanges. Partial pivoting also considers roundoff error when selecting the candidate.[ref]
For a dense n×n matrix with one right-hand side, the classical algorithm uses 32​n3+O(n2) arithmetic operations over the real numbers, counting each addition, subtraction, multiplication and division as one. At step k, the coefficient update has (n−k)2 entries, each costing one multiplication and one subtraction; the elimination multipliers, right-hand-side updates and back substitution contribute lower-order terms. Searching for partial pivoting adds O(n2) comparisons, and storing the dense coefficients uses O(n2) space. These assumptions exclude the different storage and work patterns of sparse Gaussian elimination; the exact loop counts appear in LU factorization and solve costs. Here O denotes Big O notation.
Recording the same steps as an LU decomposition makes Reusing LU factors for multiple right-hand sides possible. This is useful whenever the coefficients stay fixed while the forcing vector changes: the expensive elimination is done once. The choice of pivot element matters even when the linear system is well conditioned, as Tiny-pivot roundoff in Gaussian elimination demonstrates.

Sparse Gaussian elimination

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
Sparse Gaussian elimination solves a linear system by Gaussian elimination while exploiting its sparse matrix structure to avoid storing zeros and performing unnecessary arithmetic operations. The catch is that zeros in the input need not remain zero: eliminating a shared unknown can couple two equations that previously had no direct coupling. These new positions are fill-in, and their number can depend strongly on the order of elimination.
For a real symmetric positive-definite matrix, the usual direct method is a Cholesky decomposition. Choose an ordering, use symbolic factorization to allocate the predicted factor entries, compute their values, then solve two triangular systems. Compressed sparse storage makes the reduced storage useful. General LU decomposition may also need numerical partial pivoting, so an ordering chosen for sparsity can change during factorization.[ref]
For a fixed ordering, let P be the permutation matrix that puts the unknowns in that order. Permute both rows and columns:
B=PAPT=CCT,Cy=Pb,CTz=y,x=PTz.
(42)
Here C is the lower triangular matrix in the Cholesky decomposition of B; z=Px. Forward substitution and back substitution give the original solution. The simultaneous permutation preserves the symmetric positive-definite matrix property because vTBv=(PTv)TA(PTv)>0 for every nonzero vector v. A row permutation alone generally loses the symmetric matrix structure.
The local mechanism is a Schur complement. If the active pivot element is akk​, then for remaining indices i,j,
aijnew​=aij​−akk​aik​akj​​.
(43)
Even when aij​=0, two nonzero couplings through k make the second term nonzero. Thus the elimination graph removes k and joins its remaining neighbors into a clique. The fill-path criterion for symmetric elimination extends this local rule across several steps. The elimination tree organizes the resulting dependencies; the minimum degree algorithm and nested dissection choose orderings to control them.
This connection between graphs and linear systems was already explicit in Donald J. Rose, R. Endre Tarjan and George S. Lueker's 1976 study of fill-in and perfect elimination orderings.[ref]

Leaf elimination of a tree-pattern positive-definite matrix

Sparse Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
Associate an undirected graph with a symmetric matrix's off-diagonal nonzero pattern. Eliminating vertex i updates the remaining matrix by ajk​↦ajk​−aji​aik​/aii​. Only pairs of neighbors of i can acquire fill-in. If the graph is a tree, remove leaves successively: each eliminated vertex has at most one remaining neighbor, so only a diagonal entry can change. Every Schur complement of a positive-definite matrix is positive definite, so no zero pivot forces a different ordering. Leaf removal therefore constructs a perfect elimination ordering and a fill-free factorization.

For a symmetric factorization in a fixed ordering, the elimination tree assigns the displayed parent to a column of the lower-triangular factor when that set is nonempty. A column with no later entry is a root. The tree records dependencies of descendant updates on later pivots, supports symbolic factor allocation, and exposes parallel subtrees. It describes the factorization ordering, not merely a spanning tree of the original matrix graph.

Nested dissection

Words: 56
Sparse Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
A vertex separator divides the remaining unknowns into disconnected subdomains. Nested dissection recursively eliminates each subdomain before its separator, keeping interaction localized until late in the factorization. For a regular two-dimensional mesh with N unknowns, separators have size O(N​); the resulting direct factorization uses O(N3/2) work and O(NlogN) storage under the usual geometric separator assumptions.

At each step choose a remaining vertex of minimum degree in the current elimination graph. This heuristic reduces the size of the immediate Schur complement update and often reduces fill-in, but does not guarantee a globally optimal ordering. Its degrees must reflect earlier fill, rather than just the original graph.

Fill-in consists of new nonzero positions created by Gaussian elimination, absent from the original sparse matrix in the same ordering. For a Cholesky decomposition PAPT=CCT, compare C with the lower triangle of PAPT, not with the unpermuted input. Each new undirected edge of the elimination graph contributes one structural position in C. The sparse elimination of a four-leaf star gives six such positions when the center is eliminated first, and none when the leaves are eliminated first.

Elimination graph OurBigBook.com
After eliminating a vertex set E, a generic edge between remaining vertices i,j exists exactly when the original matrix graph contains a path from i to j whose internal vertices all belong to E. Inductively, the new edges at pivot k concatenate two such paths through k; conversely split any allowed path at k, or retain it when it avoids k. This characterizes fill by graph reachability.

Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
At each step of Gaussian elimination, select the largest absolute entry in the uneliminated part of the current column and interchange rows to put it on the diagonal. A nonsingular trailing Schur complement has a nonzero entry in its first column, so this procedure always finds a nonzero pivot in exact arithmetic. The permutation matrix P records row interchanges; earlier multipliers must be interchanged too when assembling the lower-triangular factor. This yields the LU decomposition PA=LU with unit diagonal in L. Searching within columns and interchanging rows is distinct from interchanging columns.

Row echelon form (REF)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
A matrix over a field F is in row echelon form when all zero rows follow the nonzero rows, each nonzero row's first nonzero entry lies strictly to the right of the preceding row's first nonzero entry, and all entries below each such leading entry vanish. These leading entries are its pivot elements. They need not be one, and entries above them need not vanish.[ref]
The staircase turns a linear system into a sequence of simpler equations. For example,
U=​1000​2100​−1300​​
(62)
is in row echelon form, with pivot columns 1 and 2. Its second equation determines x2​ once x3​ is chosen; its first then determines x1​ by back substitution. It is not in reduced row echelon form, because the second pivot column contains a nonzero entry above its pivot element. Neither being square nor having a nonzero entry in every row is required.
Elementary row operations bring every matrix to row echelon form: choose a nonzero entry in the leftmost available nonzero column, interchange rows, clear entries below it, and repeat on the remaining rows and later columns. Skip columns with no remaining nonzero entry. Clearing above each pivot element and scaling it to one completes reduced row echelon form.[ref]
The nonzero rows of an row echelon form are linearly independent: in a vanishing linear combination, inspecting the first pivot column forces the first coefficient to be zero, then the next forces the second, and so on. They give a basis of the original row space. The number of pivot elements is both the row rank and the column rank. To recover a basis of the original column space, select the corresponding original pivot columns; the reduced column vectors generally belong to a different column space.
Here the arithmetic is exact in the specified field. For floating-point arithmetic, deciding whether a computed entry counts as zero requires a numerical criterion; see Tiny-pivot roundoff in Gaussian elimination and condition number. An exact row echelon form classification alone does not settle numerical stability.

Two matrices of the same size over the same field are row-equivalent matrices if a sequence of elementary row operations transforms one into the other.[ref] Every operation is reversible, so they have the same row space and the same column linear relations. Writing the entire sequence as multiplication by an invertible matrix gives R=EA and
Az=0 ⟺ Rz=0,Ax=b ⟺ Rx=Eb.
(63)
Thus the kernel is preserved. For a nonzero right-hand side, perform every operation on the whole augmented matrix [A∣b]: changing the coefficients while keeping b fixed generally changes the solutions. The column space instead transforms to EcolA, which need not equal colA.

Reduced row echelon form (RREF)

Words: 616 Articles: 2
Row echelon form OurBigBook.com
A row echelon form is in reduced row echelon form when every pivot element is one and is the only nonzero entry in its column.[ref] This extra reduction displays each pivot unknown directly in terms of the free variables in a linear system. The zero matrix also satisfies the definition: it has no pivot elements.
Every matrix has exactly one reduced row echelon form under elementary row operations, with its size and column order held fixed.[ref] Ordinary row echelon form is not unique: multiplying a nonzero row by two over the rational numbers keeps the staircase but changes the matrix. The reduced conditions remove that freedom.
For a fixed number of columns, each row space has a unique reduced matrix after zero rows are removed; at a fixed full size, the number of appended zero rows is also determined. Thus reduced row echelon form represents a vector subspace independently of the starting basis. This is the uniqueness used by Gaussian binomial coefficients to count vector subspaces over a finite field.
The fixed column order matters. Elementary column operations can change the row space, the kernel and the resulting reduced row echelon form. For instance, swapping the columns of (1  2) over the rational numbers gives (2  1), whose reduced row echelon form is (1  1/2) instead of (1  2). When solving a linear system, a column interchange also requires tracking the corresponding interchange of unknowns.

which form its basis, while a3​=−7a1​+3a2​. The corresponding reduced columns are (1,0,0,0)T and (0,1,0,0)T; their linear span is a different plane. For example, every original output satisfies y3​=y1​+y2​, but (1,0,0,0)T does not. Since E is an invertible matrix, column linear relations survive EA=R even though the output vectors move. This is why choosing original columns at the reduced pivot positions works.
Uniqueness of reduced row echelon form
Words: 138
Reduced row echelon form OurBigBook.com
Here is a short proof that uses only the row space. For a vector subspace W⊆Fn, let dj​ be the dimension of its projection map onto the first j coordinates, with d0​=0. In any reduced row echelon form with row space W, dj​ counts the pivot columns among those first j columns: later-pivot rows project to zero, while earlier-pivot rows remain linearly independent. Thus the positions where dj​−dj−1​=1 determine all pivot positions from W alone.
If those positions are p1​,…,pr​, the map sending w∈W to (wp1​​,…,wpr​​) is an isomorphism W→Fr: the reduced nonzero rows map to the standard basis. Its ith row is therefore the unique vector of W with pivot-coordinate values equal to the ith standard basis vector. Any other reduced row echelon form with that row space has identical nonzero rows in identical order. At a fixed matrix size, the remaining rows must be zero. Together with existence by Gaussian elimination, this proves uniqueness.

Elementary row operation

Words: 125 Articles: 1
Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
An elementary row operation interchanges two rows of a matrix, multiplies one row by a nonzero scalar, or adds a scalar multiple of another row to it. These invertible operations are used in Gaussian elimination. For a square matrix, interchange changes the sign of its determinant, multiplication scales its determinant by the same scalar, and adding another row leaves its determinant unchanged, by multilinearity and alternation.

Elementary matrix

Words: 65
Elementary row operation OurBigBook.com
An elementary matrix is obtained by applying one elementary row operation to the identity matrix. Multiplying A by it on the left performs the same row operation on A. Such a matrix is invertible: reverse a row swap, reverse a nonzero row scaling by its reciprocal, or reverse adding a multiple of another row by adding its negative. Right multiplication gives an elementary column operation. In particular these operations preserve matrix rank.

LU decomposition (A=LU)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Numerical linear algebra OurBigBook.com
An LU decomposition writes a square matrix as A=LU, with L a lower triangular matrix and U an upper triangular matrix. We use a unit triangular matrix L, meaning lii​=1. The factors record Gaussian elimination: U contains the reduced equations, while L stores the elimination multipliers needed to reconstruct the original equations. This makes Reusing LU factors for multiple right-hand sides inexpensive.[ref]
For an invertible matrix, unpivoted LU decomposition requires nonzero pivot elements at every elimination step; invertibility alone does not guarantee this. In general use Pivoted LU decomposition, with the explicit convention PA=LU and a permutation matrix P. Once the factors exist, solving a linear system Ax=b needs forward substitution followed by back substitution, rather than forming a matrix inverse.

A=​24−2​158​134​​.

To reconstruct A from U, its second row is twice the first row of U plus the second; its third row is minus the first row of U plus three times the second plus the third. The unpivoted calculation here illustrates the structure of LU decomposition; applying partial pivoting to this particular A would choose a different first row and different factors. Both procedures can represent the same linear system when their permutation matrices are handled consistently.

A unit triangular matrix is a triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are all one. It is an invertible matrix with determinant one. In the convention used for LU decomposition, L is a unit lower triangular matrix, so forward substitution needs no division by its diagonal entries.

With unpivoted LU decomposition, P=I is the identity matrix, so the first right-hand side is simply b.[ref]
For the factors in Computed three-by-three LU decomposition and b=(7,23,26)T, forward substitution gives
y1​=7,y2​=23−2(7)=9,y3​=26+7−3(9)=6.

Forward substitution solves a linear system Ly=c with a lower triangular matrix L and nonzero diagonal, from the first row downward:
yi​=lii​ci​−∑j=1i−1​lij​yj​​,i=1,…,n.

The first sum is empty, so y1​=c1​/l11​. Each subsequent row uses only components already found. For a unit triangular matrix L, omit the division because lii​=1. The complementary procedure, back substitution, solves an upper triangular matrix system from the last row upward.[ref]

Pivoted LU decomposition (PA=LU)

Words: 275
LU decomposition OurBigBook.com
We fix the convention PA=LU: the permutation matrix P acts on the rows of A, and the same row ordering must be applied to b before the Triangular solves for LU decomposition. Equivalently, A=PTLU, since P−1=PT. LAPACK documents its factors as A=PLU instead, so check the defining equation rather than just the letter P.[ref] Partial pivoting selects the largest absolute candidate in the current column, among rows k,…,n, before forming elimination multipliers.[ref]
A zero first pivot element does not imply a singular matrix. For example,
A0​=(02​13​),detA0​=−2,P=(01​10​),PA0​=L(10​01​)​​U(20​31​)​​.
(81)
Unpivoted Gaussian elimination would divide 2 by zero. Indeed, no A0​=LU with a unit lower triangular matrix L exists: u11​=0 would force (LU)21​=l21​u11​=0, contradicting (A0​)21​=2. One row interchange resolves the obstruction. For b0​=(1,5)T, use Pb0​=(5,1)T; back substitution then gives x=(1,1)T. Using the original b0​ with these factors would solve a different linear system.
Partial pivoting bounds each elimination multiplier by one in absolute value in exact arithmetic. This helps control roundoff error, but intermediate entries can still grow; it is not an unconditional guarantee of numerical stability for every matrix.[ref] It also does not remove the original problem's condition number. For the diagonal matrix D=diag(1,ε) with 0<ε<1, the condition number in the Euclidean norm is κ2​(D)=1/ε. Row permutations preserve this condition number, because they preserve Euclidean norms. Even an exact solve changes from (1,1)T to (1,1+η/ε)T when the right-hand side changes from (1,ε)T to (1,ε+η)T. This sensitivity is a property of the linear system, not a zero-pivot element failure.[ref]

LU decomposition OurBigBook.com
When a fixed matrix A is used with several forcing or measurement vectors, compute its Pivoted LU decomposition once. Collect r right-hand sides into the columns of B=(b(1) ⋯ b(r)), and the corresponding solutions into X. Then
AX=B,LY=PB,UX=Y.
(82)
Each column undergoes the same row permutation, forward substitution and back substitution. Neither L, U nor P depends on B. This is the useful separation between preparing a linear system and applying its solution procedure repeatedly. LAPACK implements it by taking previously computed factors, permuting all right-hand sides, and performing the two triangular solves.[ref]
For the unpivoted factors in Computed three-by-three LU decomposition, take
B=​72326​024​46−8​​,Y=​796​02−2​4−22​​,X=​123​01−1​2−11​​.
(83)
Direct matrix multiplication checks all three identities LY=B, UX=Y and AX=B. The first column reproduces the previous solve; the other two use exactly the same factors. New right-hand sides can also arrive one at a time. If A changes, these stored factors generally need to be recomputed.

LU factorization and solve costs (32​n3+2rn2)

Words: 187
LU decomposition OurBigBook.com
For classical dense Gaussian elimination over the real numbers, count each scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication or division as one arithmetic operation. At step k, there are n−k elimination multipliers to divide out and (n−k)2 remaining entries, each requiring one multiplication and one subtraction. Thus this implementation's unpivoted factorization count is
F(n)=∑k=1n−1​((n−k)+2(n−k)2)=6n(n−1)(4n+1)​=32​n3+O(n2).
(84)
Here O uses Big O notation. Partial pivoting adds O(n2) comparisons and row movement, leaving the leading arithmetic count unchanged. The leading 32​n3 count agrees with the standard dense LU decomposition analysis.[ref]
With unit L, forward substitution uses n(n−1) arithmetic operations. Back substitution uses another n(n−1) plus n diagonal divisions. Together these cost 2n2−n per right-hand side; applying a stored row permutation moves n entries and requires no scalar arithmetic. In Big O notation, Reusing LU factors for multiple right-hand sides therefore costs
32​n3+2rn2+O(n2+rn),
(85)
whereas refactorizing for each of the r right-hand sides costs 32​rn3+O(rn2). For n=1000 and r=10, the leading counts are about 6.87×108 versus 6.69×109 arithmetic operations, nearly a tenfold saving. These are operation counts, not measured runtimes: memory access and optimized matrix multiplication also affect speed.[ref]

Stationary iterative method for a linear system OurBigBook.com
With A=D+L+U, the Gauss-Seidel method solves (D+L)x(k+1)=b−Ux(k). It uses each newly computed coordinate immediately in the remaining triangular solve. It is successive over-relaxation with parameter one, and converges from every start when A is a symmetric positive-definite matrix.
To solve a linear system Ax=b, split its matrix into the diagonal matrix D and the strictly lower and upper parts L,U, retaining their actual signs. Every diagonal entry must be nonzero. A sweep updates coordinates in order:
xi(k+1)​=aii​bi​−∑j<i​aij​xj(k+1)​−∑j>i​aij​xj(k)​​.
(95)
The Jacobi method uses the old vector throughout; the Gauss-Seidel method reuses each fresh coordinate. Thus the update order is part of the method.[ref]
The matrix splitting has M=D+L, N=−U, so its iteration matrix is
H=−(D+L)−1U,x(k+1)=Hx(k)+(D+L)−1b.
(96)
Compute the update by forward substitution with the lower triangular matrix D+L, rather than forming a matrix inverse. For a sparse matrix, a sweep only visits stored entries and can overwrite the working vector. Dependencies on fresh coordinates constrain parallel execution. This makes the Gauss-Seidel method an inexpensive solver component, including in a multigrid method.[ref]

Holding the other coordinates fixed, minimizing in coordinate i gives the corresponding row update. A change δi​ lowers F by exactly aii​δi2​/2. Each fresh coordinate is therefore the minimizer for the current vector, and a complete sweep lowers the quadratic form error unless every coordinate already solves its row. Convergence criterion for a stationary iteration (Hk→0⟺ρ(H)<1)

Iteration matrix OurBigBook.com
A stationary iterative method for a linear system converges to its specified fixed point for every initial vector if and only if its iteration matrix satisfies ρ(H)<1, where the spectral radius is the largest modulus of an eigenvalue.[ref]
For a diagonalizable matrix, write H=VΛV−1. Then Hk=VΛkV−1, so each eigenvector coefficient tends to zero exactly when its eigenvalue has modulus less than one. For a general matrix, the Jordan normal form gives the same result: a Jordan block J=λI+K with a nilpotent matrix K of size m satisfies
Jk=∑j=0min(k,m−1)​(jk​)λk−jKj.
(109)
If 0<∣λ∣<1, every coefficient tends to zero because exponential decay beats any fixed polynomial in k; if λ=0, the block vanishes once k≥m. Conversely, an eigenvector with ∣λ∣≥1 provides an initial error that cannot tend to zero. For a real matrix with complex eigenvalues, the same obstruction appears in the real invariant subspace spanned by the real and imaginary parts of an eigenvector.
The words "every initial vector" matter. For example, H=diag(3/2,1/2) fails the criterion, but e(0)=(0,1)T still tends to zero. Here a generic initial error has a nonzero first coordinate and diverges; the exceptional errors lie on the second coordinate axis. With H=diag(−1,1/2), generic errors oscillate rather than diverge in norm, while the same exceptional axis still converges. Both are valid matrix splittings with M=I and A=I−H. In general the convergent errors form the direct sum of the generalized eigenspaces for ∣λ∣<1; if ρ(H)≥1, this is a proper linear subspace.
A small spectral radius describes eventual convergence, but does not imply that the Euclidean norm of the error decreases on every step for a non-normal matrix. An operator norm bound ∥H∥<1 does give the stepwise estimate ∥e(k)∥≤∥H∥k∥e(0)∥. For a real symmetric matrix, the matrix 2-norm equals its spectral radius, making this particularly direct.

(110)
Keeping A fixed, the approximate vector exactly solves Ax(k)=b+δb with δb=−r(k). Thus, for b=0, ∥r(k)∥/∥b∥ is the relative backward error when only the right-hand side may change. For a vector norm and its induced operator norm,
∥x∗​∥∥e(k)∥​≤κ(A)∥b∥∥r(k)∥​,κ(A)=∥A∥∥A−1∥.
(111)
A small relative linear-system residual ensures a small relative forward error when the condition number is moderate; an ill-conditioned matrix can amplify it. The bound follows directly from e=−A−1r and ∥b∥=∥Ax∗​∥≤∥A∥∥x∗​∥.[ref]
For the Jacobi iteration for a three-variable tridiagonal system, the first linear-system residual is (1,3,1)T, while the first forward error is (−1/2,−1,−1/2)T. In the Euclidean norm, the relative forward error is 3/28​≈0.3273 and the relative linear-system residual is 11/120​≈0.3028. Its spectral condition number of a positive-definite matrix is (4+2​)/(4−2​)≈2.094, so the bound is about 0.6340. The bound is a guarantee, not an equality. In floating-point arithmetic, recompute the linear-system residual from the current vector when checking termination; a small update alone need not certify a small forward error.

Matrix splitting

Words: 235 Articles: 1
Stationary iterative method for a linear system OurBigBook.com
A splitting A=M−N with invertible M produces
x(k+1)=M−1Nx(k)+M−1b.
(112)
A matrix splitting chooses an easy part M of a matrix and corrects for the remaining part N. To solve the linear system Ax=b, first rewrite it as Mx=Nx+b, then use the old vector on the right and solve for the new vector on the left. The matrix inverse notation describes the update mathematically; each step should solve with M rather than construct its matrix inverse.[ref]
The same identity also yields a correction based on the linear-system residual:
x(k+1)=x(k)+M−1(b−Ax(k)),H=I−M−1A.
(113)
This connects a matrix splitting to matrix preconditioning: M−1 rescales the imbalance before adding a correction. Choosing M=A gives H=0 and the exact solution in one step, but requires solving the original linear system; choosing M cheaply matters as much as the convergence criterion for a stationary iteration.
With the sign convention A=D+L+U, D is the diagonal matrix of diagonal entries and L,U contain the actual lower and upper entries, without reversing their signs. The Jacobi method uses M=D, N=−(L+U); the Gauss-Seidel method uses M=D+L, N=−U. The first requires only division by diagonal entries; the second uses a lower triangular matrix and forward substitution. These choices explain their different information flows.

Householder-John theorem

Words: 32
Matrix splitting OurBigBook.com
Let A=M−N be Hermitian positive definite. If M∗+N is also Hermitian positive definite, then M is invertible and
ρ(M−1N)<1.
(114)
Thus the stationary iteration associated with the splitting converges from every initial vector.

Jacobi method

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Stationary iterative method for a linear system OurBigBook.com
Writing A=D+L+U, where D is diagonal and L,U are strictly triangular, the Jacobi iteration is
x(k+1)=D−1(b−(L+U)x(k)).
(115)
The Jacobi method solves a linear system by updating every coordinate from the same old vector. It requires every diagonal entry aii​ to be nonzero. Isolating coordinate i in row i gives the simultaneous rule
xi(k+1)​=aii​bi​−∑j=i​aij​xj(k)​​,B=−D−1(L+U)=I−D−1A.
(116)
Here B is the iteration matrix. A sweep computes a complete new vector before replacing the old one, so its coordinate updates can run independently.[ref]
For a sparse matrix, a sweep needs work proportional to the stored nonzero entries, while Gaussian elimination may create fill-in. The Jacobi method is therefore a simple starting point for large linear systems, and the weighted Jacobi method supplies a useful building block of a multigrid method. Its beauty is that a local row correction becomes a global eigenvalue question: the convergence criterion for a stationary iteration is exactly ρ(B)<1.

Jacobi iteration for a three-variable tridiagonal system (ρ(B)=2​/4)

Words: 277 Articles: 1
Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
Consider the original linear system with a symmetric matrix that is also a tridiagonal matrix:
A=​4−10​−14−1​0−14​​,x∗​=​123​​,b=Ax∗​=​2410​​.
(117)
Here D=4I and the Jacobi method reads
x1(k+1)​=42+x2(k)​​,x2(k+1)​=44+x1(k)​+x3(k)​​,x3(k+1)​=410+x2(k)​​.
(118)
Starting from x(0)=0, the first three vectors are
x(1)=​1/215/2​​,x(2)=​3/47/411/4​​,x(3)=​15/1615/847/16​​.
(119)
Every right-hand side uses superscript k, including the middle row, even when a new first coordinate has already been computed.
For comparison, a first Gauss-Seidel method sweep in coordinate order 1,2,3 gives
x1(1)​=42​=21​,x2(1)​=44+1/2+0​=89​,x3(1)​=410+9/8​=3289​.
(120)
The new first coordinate enters the middle update, and the new second coordinate enters the final update. Accidentally overwriting old coordinates during a Jacobi method sweep therefore changes the mathematical method.
Error modes of a three-variable Jacobi iteration (e(k)=Bke(0))
Words: 169
Jacobi iteration for a three-variable tridiagonal system OurBigBook.com
For the Jacobi iteration for a three-variable tridiagonal system,
B=41​​010​101​010​​.
(121)
An orthonormal eigenbasis is
u+​=21​​12​1​​,u0​=2​1​​10−1​​,u−​=21​​1−2​1​​,
(122)
with eigenvalues q=2​/4, 0, and −q, respectively. These are error modes: their shapes persist under the iteration matrix, while their coefficients change. Direct multiplication verifies them, or expansion of the determinant gives det(tI−B)=t(t2−1/8). Thus ρ(B)=q<1 and convergence holds for every starting vector.
With x(0)=0, the initial forward error has coefficients
e(0)=−x∗​=c+​u+​+c0​u0​+c−​u−​,c+​=−2−2​,c0​=2​,c−​=−2+2​.
(123)
For k≥1,
e(k)=c+​qku+​+c−​(−q)ku−​,∥e(k)∥2​=23​qk.
(124)
The zero mode disappears after one sweep; the negative mode alternates in sign. The Euclidean norm drops by exactly q per sweep from k=1 onward. The first norm drop is different because ∥e(0)∥2​=14​ includes the zero mode. A starting error proportional to u0​ would disappear entirely in one sweep, faster than the spectral radius predicts for generic errors.
The curves are computed iterates and exact formulas for this linear system. Since A=4(I−B), the same eigenvectors have eigenvalues 4−2​, 4, and 4+2​ for A. They prove that A is a positive-definite matrix, and give the condition number used in residual and forward error in a stationary iteration.

Jacobi convergence from strict diagonal dominance (∥B∥∞​=maxi​∑j=i​∣aij​/aii​∣<1)

Words: 138
Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
A strictly diagonally dominant matrix guarantees convergence of the Jacobi method for every initial vector.[ref]
Indeed, using the maximum norm ∥v∥∞​=maxi​∣vi​∣, the induced operator norm is the largest absolute row sum. The Jacobi method has bii​=0 and bij​=−aij​/aii​ for j=i, so
ρ(B)≤∥B∥∞​=maxi​∣aii​∣∑j=i​∣aij​∣​<1,∥e(k)∥∞​≤∥B∥∞k​∥e(0)∥∞​.
(125)
This gives a cheap sufficient check without computing any eigenvalues. For the Jacobi iteration for a three-variable tridiagonal system, the absolute row sums of B are 1/4,1/2,1/4, giving ∥B∥∞​=1/2. The true spectral radius 2​/4 gives a sharper eventual rate.
Strict diagonal dominance is sufficient, not necessary: A=(11/10​21​) violates it in the first row, but its Jacobi method has eigenvalues ±1/5​ and converges. Conversely, being a positive-definite matrix alone is insufficient: the Jacobi convergence for a three-by-three equicorrelation matrix with α=3/4 has positive eigenvalues 5/2,1/4,1/4 for A, but spectral radius 3/2 for its iteration matrix. The extra tridiagonal matrix structure in Jacobi convergence for a symmetric positive-definite tridiagonal matrix is therefore substantive.

Skew-tridiagonal Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterations

Words: 53
Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
For A=μ−1I+U−UT, with U the four-dimensional unit superdiagonal, the Jacobi method has eigenvalues 2iμcos(jπ/5), j=1,…,4. The Gauss-Seidel method has two zero eigenvalues and −μ2(3±5​)/2. Therefore both methods converge for every starting vector exactly when 0<∣μ∣<(5​−1)/2. This equality of convergence ranges follows from their spectra, not from positive-definiteness of the nonsymmetric coefficient matrix.

Weighted Jacobi method

Words: 341 Articles: 4
Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
With relaxation parameter ω, weighted Jacobi updates by
x(ν+1)=x(ν)+ωD−1(b−Ax(ν)).
(126)
Its iteration matrix is Hω​=I−ωD−1A.
Equivalently, the weighted Jacobi method takes a weighted average of the old vector and its full Jacobi method update: x(k+1)=(1−ω)x(k)+ωxJacobi(k+1)​. If Bv=λv, its iteration matrix multiplies that eigenvector by 1−ω+ωλ. For the diagonal-4 Jacobi iteration for a three-variable tridiagonal system, the factors are 1−ω and 1−ω±ω2​/4; a Poisson equation smoothing parameter must not be inferred from this different matrix.
Weighted Jacobi eigenvalues for a square Dirichlet grid (λk,l​(Hω​))
Words: 35
Weighted Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
For the five-point discretization of −Δ+c on the unit square, the weighted iteration eigenvalues are 1−ω[4sin2(πkh/2)+4sin2(πlh/2)+ch2]/(4+ch2). A fixed parameter converges for every mesh when 0<ω≤1, but ω=1 poorly damps the highest frequencies.
Weighted Jacobi method for the one-dimensional Poisson equation
Words: 241 Articles: 2
Weighted Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
For the centered second-difference matrix with diagonal −2 and off-diagonals 1, the weighted-Jacobi eigenvalues are
λk​(ω)=1−ω+ωcosn+1kπ​,1≤k≤n.
(127)
The method converges for every grid size exactly when 0<ω≤1.
Multiplying both A and b by −1 leaves D−1A and the weighted Jacobi method unchanged. Thus the same formula applies to the positive second-difference matrix Tn​ with diagonal 2 and neighboring entries −1, the finite difference form of the one-dimensional Poisson equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Its eigenvectors have components sin(jkπ/(n+1)), and D−1Tn​ has eigenvalues 1−cos(kπ/(n+1)). At ω=2/3, upper-half modes have factors between −1/3 and 1/3, while low-frequency factors remain close to one on fine grids. This explains why the weighted Jacobi method helps a multigrid method by reducing oscillatory errors, even when it is a slow solver on its own.[ref]
High-frequency smoothing factor of weighted Jacobi (μω​)
Words: 106 Articles: 1
Weighted Jacobi method for the one-dimensional Poisson equation OurBigBook.com
For modes with k/(n+1)∈[1/2,1] and large n, the worst attenuation factor is
μω​=max{∣1−ω∣,∣1−2ω∣}.
(128)
It is minimized by ω=2/3, for which μω​=1/3.
Exact finite-grid high-frequency Jacobi smoothing optimum (ω∗​=2/(a+b),μ∗​=(b−a)/(a+b))
Words: 82
High-frequency smoothing factor of weighted Jacobi OurBigBook.com
For the one-dimensional Dirichlet second-difference grid, high sine modes have eigenvalues 1−ωtk​, with tk​=1−cos(kπ/(n+1)) and k≥⌈(n+1)/2⌉. Let a and b be the smallest and largest of these tk​. Convexity gives attenuation max(∣1−ωa∣,∣1−ωb∣). Balancing its endpoint values with opposite signs gives the displayed exact minimax choice. For odd n, a=1; for even n, a=1+sin(π/[2(n+1)]), and always b=1+cos(π/(n+1)). Only in the large-grid or uniform-in-grid limit do these become ω∗​=2/3, μ∗​=1/3.

Jacobi convergence for a three-by-three equicorrelation matrix

Words: 46
Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
For a three-by-three matrix with diagonal entries one and every off-diagonal entry α, the Jacobi method iteration matrix has eigenvalue −2α on the all-ones vector and eigenvalue α with multiplicity two on its orthogonal complement. Its spectral radius is 2∣α∣, so Jacobi iteration converges exactly when ∣α∣<1/2.

Jacobi convergence for a symmetric positive-definite tridiagonal matrix

Words: 28
Jacobi method OurBigBook.com
If A=D+L+LT is symmetric positive definite and tridiagonal, set S=diag(1,−1,1,−1,…). Then
SAS=D−L−LT
(129)
is positive definite. Applying the Householder-John theorem to M=D and N=−(L+LT) proves that the Jacobi iteration converges.
